claims.text: High-temperature thermodynamic stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by the energetic benefits of atomic mixing.
High-temperature kinetic stability of these nanoparticles is governed by kinetic barriers to phase separation.
Molecular dynamics simulations over 773–1923 K can investigate nanoparticle thermodynamic and kinetic stability.
The proposed service regime spans 773–1923 K and includes catalytic settings with low noble-metal content.
Atomic mixing and phase separation are the structural mediators of stability.
Molecular dynamics modeling constitutes the mechanism of nanoparticle behavior and properties.
Higher entropy of mixing improves structural and chemical stability at high temperature.
Lower kinetic barriers to phase separation improve structural and chemical stability at high temperature.
Low entropy of mixing produces poor structural and chemical stability at high temperature.
High kinetic barriers to phase separation produce poor structural and chemical stability at high temperature.
The hypothesis applies broadly to multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles of varying compositions and structures over 773–1923 K.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes kinetic barriers to phase separation as a stabilizing competition against separation, but the prediction assigns improved stability to lower barriers and the baseline assigns poor stability to higher barriers. Lower barriers would ordinarily facilitate phase separation, so the stated direction is internally incoherent absent an additional explanation.

The structural mediator names physical processes, whereas the mechanism names molecular dynamics, which is an investigative method rather than a physical mechanism connecting mixing or separation to stability.
